nameStory: The Lesser Shining Bobtail gets its name from its small size compared to other bobtail squids, and the shimmering, iridescent quality of its skin that seems to shine underwater. 'Bobtail' refers to its stubby, rounded body shape that's much shorter than the elongated bodies of typical squids.
description: The Lesser Shining Bobtail is a tiny, rounded squid that looks more like a miniature octopus than the long-bodied squids most people know. These petite cephalopods grow to about 2 inches in mantle length (the main body part), making them one of the smaller squids in New England waters. They have the characteristic eight arms of their squid relatives, but their body is distinctly stubby and rounded rather than torpedo-shaped. Their skin has an iridescent quality that can shimmer with changing colors.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly rounded and stubby body, much shorter and wider than typical squids - almost octopus-like in proportions

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, reaching only about 2 inches in total mantle length when fully grown

idTips.label: Skin Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, soft skin with an iridescent, shimmering quality that reflects light underwater

idTips.label: Arms
idTips.description: Eight relatively short arms compared to body size, without the long feeding tentacles of larger squids

idTips.label: Color Changes
idTips.description: Can rapidly change colors and patterns across its skin surface, often displaying mottled browns and translucent patches

habitat: Lesser Shining Bobtails live in deeper waters of the Gulf of Maine and along New England's continental shelf, typically in sandy or muddy bottom areas. They're rarely seen in shallow coastal waters, preferring the cooler, deeper ocean environment beyond the reach of most casual divers or snorkelers.

seasonality.spring: May be found in deeper Gulf of Maine waters as ocean temperatures begin to warm, though sightings remain extremely rare.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season for encounters in New England waters, when warmer temperatures may bring them into slightly shallower areas of the continental shelf.
seasonality.fall: Still present in deeper waters as temperatures begin to cool, continuing their secretive lifestyle in sandy bottom habitats.
seasonality.winter: Remain in deeper, more stable temperature waters of the Gulf of Maine, well below the reach of most observers.

funFact: Despite being called a 'squid,' bobtails are actually more closely related to cuttlefish and have a tiny internal shell-like structure called a gladius, plus they can bury themselves in sand with just their eyes peeking out like tiny periscopes!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for a very small octopus due to its rounded body shape, but bobtail squids have ten arms total (eight regular arms plus two shorter tentacles) while octopuses have only eight arms. The iridescent, shimmering skin is also more pronounced than most small octopuses.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'bobtail squid' can be confusing because these animals are actually more closely related to cuttlefish than to true squids, despite the common name. They belong to their own distinct order and have evolved a very different lifestyle from their torpedo-shaped squid cousins.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in New England waters, the Lesser Shining Bobtail would need to be compared with other small cephalopods in the region. It's much smaller and more rounded than any true squids found locally, and lacks the complex fin arrangements seen in cuttlefish relatives from warmer waters.
